> **The research decision.** Which group your observed data can honestly speak for,
> and where exactly the line falls past which a description of your sample is no
> longer allowed to become a claim about a wider population. You draw that line, and
> you write down the sentence on the far side of it that you refuse to say.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: which group your data can honestly speak for.**

Picture a policy stakeholder reading your report before deciding whether it applies to
their city. Their first question is never about your math. It is: *"Which group did
your procedure actually reach?"* A result that quietly describes one group while
claiming to speak for another is the most common failure in observational work: an
estimate that is precise, well-formatted, and about the wrong group. This chapter
equips you to name the group your data reach, and to refuse the sentence that swaps it
for a group your data never touched.

## The concept

This chapter follows the observational-descriptive pathway of the design library in
RDSS [@blair2023rdss]. **Observational descriptive research** means you sample and
measure without assigning anyone a condition, then summarize what you found. Example:
you pull the roll call records of every member of a legislature and report how often
each one crossed party lines. Because its inquiry and its answer strategy are
descriptive, this pathway estimates distributions and relationships, and with care
generalizes them to a population. Those estimates do not by themselves identify a
causal effect. The next chapter takes the other road: observational data again, no
assignment again, but a causal inquiry that has to carry an identification argument
to earn its answer.

Four groups keep such a description honest [@groves2009survey]. They are often drawn
as boxes inside boxes, and that picture is worth knowing along with the place it
lies.

- **Target population**: everyone your question is about. Example: every customer a
  streaming service will ever bill. This is the group you wish you could study.
- **Accessible population**: the part of the target you could reach in principle,
  given time and cost. Example: the customers you can actually contact with a survey
  this quarter.
- **Sampling frame**: the concrete list you actually draw from. Example: the current
  subscriber list your survey tool pulls from. This is the box that misbehaves, in
  three ways worth naming. **Undercoverage** is people who belong in your target
  and never make the list. **Overcoverage** is records on the list for people
  outside your target altogether. A **duplicate** is one person listed twice, which
  quietly gives them two chances of being picked. Treating the frame as a clean
  slice of the population above it is one of the quietest ways a description goes
  wrong.
- **Sample**: the customers you actually survey, drawn from the frame and no wider.

![The four groups a description has to keep straight. The frame crosses the edge of
your target population, which is where the three coverage errors live: people inside
the target who never reach the list, records on the list that fall outside the target
altogether, and one unit listed
twice.](../images/concepts/sampling_groups.png){fig-alt="Diagram of overlapping
regions. A large box is the target population; inside it, a shaded box is the
accessible population. A dashed box, the sampling frame, starts inside those and
extends out past the right edge of the target population. The sample is a solid box
inside the frame. Three labels point into the picture: the part of the target never
listed on the frame is undercoverage; the part of the frame outside the target is
overcoverage; and two joined dots inside the frame are one unit listed twice, a
duplicate."}

A claim is honest only when the box it describes matches the box it names. Two
processes decide how the boxes differ. **Selection** is any process that decides who
lands in your data instead of chance alone. Example: a survey taken outside one dining
hall selects for people who eat there at lunch. **Nonresponse** is the units you drew
who never gave you data. Example: of 500 people contacted, 300 reply, and the 200
silent ones are rarely a random slice. When either process relates to the very thing
you are measuring, your summary drifts from the truth, and no amount of extra data
pulls it back [@bethlehem2010selection]. Size shrinks the sample-to-sample wobble. It does nothing to a
systematic tilt in who you reached [@meng2018paradises].

## A worked example

A subscription streaming service measures its **billing-error rate**, meaning the
fraction of customers whose monthly charge comes out wrong. Example: 2 wrong charges
in 100 customers is a 2% billing-error rate. The analytics team pulls the current
subscriber list, emails a short survey to a random draw from that list, and counts how
many report a wrong charge in the past year. The survey reports 2%, and the headline
writes itself: *"the service has a 2% billing-error rate."*

Now walk the boxes. The **target population** is every customer the service bills [@groves2009survey]. The
**sampling frame** is the current subscriber list, because only people on that list
receive the survey. Here is the trap: the customers hit hardest by billing errors, the
ones charged twice or charged after canceling, are also the ones most likely to have
quit in frustration. They removed themselves from the frame before anyone surveyed
them. This is **survivorship selection**, a filter that keeps exactly the people least
likely to show the problem you are counting. Current subscribers are the contented end
of the customer base, not a fair slice of it.

So the 2% is honest about one box and dishonest about another. The licensed claim is:
*"among customers still subscribed, the billing-error rate is 2%."* The silent upgrade,
the sentence to refuse, is: *"the service's billing-error rate is 2%."* The true rate
across everyone billed is almost certainly higher, because the worst-hit customers
were gone before the survey went out. That gap between the box you measured and the
box you named is the subject of this chapter.

The block below builds the whole customer base, lets the worst-hit customers quit, and then reports what a perfect survey of the remaining list would find. Nothing here is a sampling error.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

n = 50_000
# Everyone the service bills. Wrong charges are what we want to count.
wrong_charge = rng.random(n) < 0.060
# Customers hit by a wrong charge quit far more often — and quitters leave the
# subscriber list, which is the frame the survey draws from.
quit = rng.random(n) < np.where(wrong_charge, 0.70, 0.09)

target_rate = wrong_charge.mean()
frame_rate = wrong_charge[~quit].mean()
print(f"target population (everyone billed)   : {target_rate*100:.1f}%")
print(f"sampling frame (current subscribers)  : {frame_rate*100:.1f}%")
print(f"customers who left the frame          : {quit.mean()*100:.0f}%")
print("\nthe survey can only ever see the second number. no sample size,")
print("and no random draw from that list, closes the gap to the first")
```

## A seeded simulation

The worked example argues that *who you reach* tilts *what you measure*, and
that a bigger sample does not fix the tilt. You can watch that happen. A
**seed** is a fixed starting point for a random-number generator: the same
seed always reproduces the same draws, so the figure below is exactly what
you will get when you run this code in the companion notebook. The code
builds a population of 100,000 people whose true mean age is known by
construction, draws ten honest random samples of 500, then draws one
convenience sample of the same size through a channel that mostly reaches
younger people.

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

population = np.clip(rng.normal(49, 17, size=100_000), 18, 90)
truth = population.mean()

random_means = [rng.choice(population, 500, replace=False).mean()
                for _ in range(10)]

weights = np.exp(-(population - 25) ** 2 / (2 * 12 ** 2))  # younger = likelier
convenience = rng.choice(population, 500, replace=False,
                         p=weights / weights.sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 2.9))
ax.scatter(random_means, np.ones(10), s=60, color="#2a78d6", zorder=3)
ax.scatter([convenience.mean()], [0], s=60, color="#eb6834", zorder=3)
ax.axvline(truth, color="#333333", ls="--", lw=1.2)
ax.text(truth + .5, 1.55, f"true mean = {truth:.1f}", color="#333333",
        fontsize=9)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1], ["Convenience\nchannel (n = 500)",
                       "Random samples\n(n = 500)"], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("Sample mean age (years)")
ax.set_ylim(-.7, 1.9)
plt.show()
```

![Ten random sample means cluster around the true mean age; the single
convenience-channel mean sits far below
it.](../images/sims/ch11_sampling_channels.png){fig-alt="Dot plot. Ten blue
random-sample means huddle between about 47 and 51 around a dashed line at
the true mean of 49.1. A single orange convenience-channel mean sits alone at
about 33."}

Read it the way a reviewer would. The ten random samples never agree exactly:
their means spread between about 47 and 51. But they huddle around the truth,
and that spread is honest, quantifiable uncertainty. The convenience channel
has exactly the same sample size, and it misses the true mean by about
sixteen years. Nothing about the dot itself warns you; it looks as confident
as any other. Only the sampling *procedure* tells you which kind of dot you
have. In the companion notebook, move the channel's center (the `25` inside
`weights`) and rerun: the tilt follows the channel, never the sample size.

## Description over time

A labor ministry reports that the average hourly wage of employed workers rose 2.6%
during a recession. Nobody at the ministry made an arithmetic error, and nobody's pay
went up. The number moved because the group it describes changed underneath it. That
is the first thing to check whenever a description has a date on it.

Two designs collect the same kind of number over time, and they reach different
groups. A **repeated cross-section** is a fresh sample drawn from the population at
each point in time. Example: a national labor survey that interviews a new random set
of households every month. A **panel** is one sample of units followed and measured
again and again. Example: a study that re-interviews the same 3,000 households every
year for a decade [@lynn2009methodology]. The repeated cross-section licenses a
sentence about the population *as it stood* at each date. The panel licenses a
sentence about how the units you started with changed, which is the only design of
the two that can see any one household's path. Those units stand for the population as it
stood when the panel was drawn. A household formed five years later is not in it unless
the study adds new members along the way.

Each design has its own way of misleading you. A repeated cross-section's averages
fold in **composition change**, meaning a shift in a group's average that comes from who
belongs to the group, not from any member changing. Example: when lower-paid workers
lose their jobs first, the average wage of the people still employed rises, even though
every remaining worker earns exactly what they earned before. That shift is a true fact
about the population. It misleads only when you read it as a change in what people are
paid. A panel suffers from **attrition**, meaning units that drop out between waves.
Example: a household that moves away after the second interview never answers the
third. Attrition is the same survivorship selection that removed the angriest customers
from the streaming service's subscriber list, because the households that move, fall
ill, or stop answering are rarely a random slice. Panels also suffer from **panel conditioning**,
meaning that being asked the same questions repeatedly changes how people behave or
answer. Example: a household asked every month about its savings starts paying closer
attention to them.

The block below builds a workforce in which no wage ever changes, lets a downturn take
jobs mostly from the lower-paid, and compares the two designs.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

n = 20_000
# Each worker's hourly wage is FIXED. Nobody gets a raise or a cut.
wage_before = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(22), sigma=0.45, size=n)
wage_after = wage_before.copy()
# In the downturn, lower-paid workers lose their jobs far more often.
low_paid = wage_before < np.median(wage_before)
lose_job = rng.random(n) < np.where(low_paid, 0.18, 0.04)

before = wage_before.mean()             # everyone employed before
after = wage_after[~lose_job].mean()    # whoever is employed after
panel = (wage_after - wage_before)[~lose_job].mean()  # same people, followed

print(f"mean wage of the employed, before : ${before:.2f}")
print(f"mean wage of the employed, after  : ${after:.2f}")
print(f"change in the headline average    : {100*(after/before - 1):+.1f}%")
print(f"workers who left the employed pool: {lose_job.mean()*100:.0f}%")
print(f"panel: change for workers followed: ${panel:.2f}")
print("\nthe average rose because WHO is employed changed,")
print("not because anyone was paid more")
```

The headline average climbs from \$24.31 to \$24.94, a 2.6% rise, after 11% of workers
leave the employed pool. The panel of workers who kept their jobs shows a change of
exactly zero. Both numbers are correct. They answer different questions, and only
your sentence decides which one you are asking.

Two more traps sit in any series. The first is **serial dependence**, meaning that each
period's value is tied to the one before it. Example: a store's sales in March look a
lot like its sales in February, because the same customers, prices, and staff carry
over. When consecutive months move together like this, twenty-four monthly values
hold less independent information than twenty-four separate draws, and an interval
for their average computed as if they were independent comes out too narrow. The second is the **base
period** of an index, meaning the date the index is set to 100 so later values read as
change from it. Example: a price index based in a year when prices had dipped puts
every later year well above 100, so "prices are up 30% since the base year" sounds
dramatic even though the change from one year to the next is exactly the same under
any base. Name the base period, and check whether a different, equally defensible one
changes your sentence.

An AI tool is fast at the mechanical part of this work. It can split a series by who
entered and who left, recompute an index on a new base period, or draft the table that
sets the stayers' wages beside the leavers'. It is weak at the sentence. Ask a chatbot
to summarize the wage series and it can easily write that wages rose, a **silent
scope change** from "the average among the employed" to "what workers are paid."
Which group the number describes is your call, and you check the tool's summary
against it.

A description over time declares its estimand in words: the population's average at
each date, or the average change for the units you followed. Its warrant is the same
sampling license as the rest of this chapter, applied once per wave, plus a documented
account of who left a panel. What it cannot establish is *why* the series moved.
Attributing a break in the line to a policy that arrived that month is a causal claim,
and it needs a design built for it. The interrupted time series in
[Natural Experiments](../part7-further-routes/natural-experiments.qmd) is where that
claim gets its argument.

## Description over space

A state health department publishes a county map of a tick-borne disease. The darkest
counties sit in one corner of the state, and a reporter writes that the corner is a
hot spot. Before you repeat that sentence, ask three questions of the map: what the
color divides by, how big each county is, and where the lines were drawn.

The first question is about the denominator. A **rate** is a count divided by the
number of people who could have produced it. Example: 12 cases among 30,000 residents
is 40 cases per 100,000. A map of raw counts is mostly a map of where people live,
since big counties have more of everything. When your question is about risk, map the
rate and state its denominator in the legend. Map the count only when the question is
where the most cases are, for example to decide where to send clinic staff.

The second question is about size. A small county's rate rests on very few people, so
chance alone swings it far above or below the truth. The block below gives every one
of 300 counties exactly the same true rate, 40 cases per 100,000 residents, then counts
the cases chance produces.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# 300 counties, from tiny to large. The TRUE rate is identical everywhere:
# 40 cases per 100,000 residents. No county is riskier than any other.
pop = np.round(np.exp(rng.uniform(np.log(1_000), np.log(500_000), 300))).astype(int)
cases = rng.poisson(pop * 40 / 100_000)
rate = cases / pop * 100_000

counties = pd.DataFrame({"pop": pop, "rate": rate})
highest = counties.nlargest(10, "rate")     # the darkest counties
zero = counties[counties["rate"] == 0]      # the palest: no cases at all
print(f"true rate in every county           : 40.0 per 100,000")
print(f"median county population            : {np.median(pop):,.0f}")
print(f"10 highest observed rates           : median pop {highest['pop'].median():,.0f}, "
      f"largest {highest['pop'].max():,}")
print(f"{len(zero)} counties with zero cases         : median pop {zero['pop'].median():,.0f}, "
      f"largest {zero['pop'].max():,}")
print(f"lowest / highest observed rate      : {rate.min():.1f} / {rate.max():.1f}")
print("\nthe darkest and the palest counties on the map are")
print("the smallest ones: the map is showing you noise")
```

The typical county has about 28,500 residents. The ten counties with the highest
observed rates have a median of about 1,500 residents, and none has more than 4,955.
At the other end, 23 counties recorded no cases at all; their median is about 2,400
residents, and the largest has 6,413. Observed rates run from 0 to about 197 per
100,000 in a state where every county's true rate is 40. Both ends of the color scale
belong to the smallest places.
Before you call a county a hot spot, put its population and an interval beside its
rate.

The third question is about the lines. The **modifiable areal unit problem** is the
fact that a summary computed over areas can change when you redraw the areas or change
their size, even though no person moved. Example: the link between income and turnout
computed across a state's counties can differ from the same link computed across the
precincts inside them, with exactly the same voters. Fotheringham and Wong showed that
regression estimates computed on grouped data shift with both the size and the layout
of the zones, in ways that are hard to predict in advance
[@fotheringham1991modifiable]. When you can, rerun the summary at a second scale or on
a second set of boundaries. If your finding appears at one scale only, report the
scale in the claim.

Places also break a rule that most interval formulas assume: that the observations are
independent. **Spatial autocorrelation** means that nearby places tend to have similar
values. Example: neighboring counties share weather, deer populations, and commuters,
so their tick counts rise and fall together. The geographer Waldo Tobler put it as a
law: near things are more related than distant things [@tobler1970computer]. For you
it means that 300 counties are not 300 independent observations when neighbors share
what drives their numbers. An interval for a statewide average or trend computed as if
they were independent usually comes out narrower than the evidence supports, which is
the same trap serial dependence sets in a time series.

The last trap is about people. The **ecological fallacy** is reading a relationship
measured across areas as if it held among the individuals inside them. Robinson's classic case
measured it with a **correlation**, a number from −1 to 1 that says how closely two
quantities rise and fall together. Example: 0 means no straight-line link, and a
negative value means one tends to be high where the other is low. Robinson used United
States census data from 1930. Across individuals, being born abroad was slightly
positively correlated with being unable to read (0.118). Across the 48 states, the
share born abroad and the share unable to read were *negatively* correlated (−0.526)
[@robinson1950ecological]. The state correlation also depends on things the individual
one ignores, such as where immigrants settled and how well everyone else in those
states could read, so it can point the opposite way from the pattern among people. The
state numbers were accurate, and they answered a question about states. Read as a
statement about people, they pointed the wrong way.

So a spatial description declares its estimand as a rate for each area, or a summary
across areas, and states its unit (counties, not residents), its denominator, its
scale, and an interval that respects neighbors. Its warrant runs to the areas you
covered, at the boundaries you used. It cannot tell you which individuals are at risk,
and it cannot tell you why one place differs from its neighbor. An AI tool can build a
**choropleth**, a map that shades each area by its value, in seconds. It may also label
the darkest cluster a hot spot with no interval and no population beside it. That label is a claim you check, not a finding you inherit. When
the question becomes why two neighboring places differ after one of them changed a
rule, it has turned causal, and comparisons across a border are one of the designs in
[Natural Experiments](../part7-further-routes/natural-experiments.qmd).

## A language model is not a sample of people

A political scientist wants to know how warmly voters feel toward a party. A
chatbot offers to answer the questionnaire a thousand times, "as" a thousand voters
with different ages, incomes, and home states. The answers arrive in minutes, tidy
and cheap. It is tempting to treat them as survey data. Resist that temptation.

Political scientists have tested this idea directly. Argyle and colleagues coined the term
**silicon sample**, meaning a set of answers generated by a language model that has
been told to respond as a person with a given background. Example: prompting a model
with "I am a 45-year-old retired teacher from Ohio" before each survey question. They
built the backgrounds from thousands of real participants in large United States
surveys and reported that, conditioned this way, the GPT-3 model reproduced the answer
patterns of many demographic subgroups closely. They called that property
**algorithmic fidelity** and argued that a model is useful as a stand-in only to the
extent that it has enough of it for the question at hand [@argyle2023out]. Bisbee and
colleagues then gave ChatGPT personas copied from the backgrounds of real survey
respondents, asked it to rate eleven social and political groups, and compared its
answers with what the people had said. The synthetic averages were close to the
survey's. The synthetic answers varied far less than real ones, relationships estimated
from them often differed from the relationships in the human data, and the results
shifted with small changes in prompt wording and when the same prompt was run again
three months later. They concluded that the synthetic answers were not reliable for
statistical inference [@bisbee2024synthetic].

The deeper problem is the one this whole chapter is about: which group do the numbers
speak for? Notice what was sampled in both studies. The *backgrounds* were copied from
real respondents, so the mix of ages, incomes, and states in the prompts can match a
probability sample of voters. The *answers* were not drawn from those voters. The model
wrote every one of them. A sampling license covers what was sampled, so here it covers
the list of personas, and nothing connects the ratings themselves to any population of
people. Only a check against real answers, question by question, can show how close
they come. The reach of the answers is the model itself, at one version, on one date,
with one prompt, one set of personas, and one set of generation settings. The block
below makes that concrete with constructed numbers, not ones taken from any study.

```python
import numpy as np
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# CONSTRUCTED for illustration, not taken from any study:
# people rate a political group on a 0-100 "feeling thermometer."
people = np.clip(rng.normal(55, 26, 1_000), 0, 100)
# A model asked to answer "as" 1,000 personas lands near the same
# average but squeezes everyone toward the middle.
silicon = np.clip(rng.normal(57, 8, 1_000), 0, 100)

for name, x in [("people ", people), ("silicon", silicon)]:
    se = x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x))
    print(f"{name}: mean {x.mean():5.1f}  (95% interval "
          f"{x.mean()-1.96*se:4.1f} to {x.mean()+1.96*se:4.1f})  "
          f"share above 80: {100*(x > 80).mean():4.1f}%")
print("\nthe averages look alike; the spread, and every claim built on it,")
print("does not. the silicon interval is about the model, not about people")
```

The two averages differ by about a point: 55.8 for the people and 57.0 for the silicon
answers. Everything built on the spread comes apart. Among the people, 17.9% give a
rating above 80. Among the silicon answers, 0.2% do. The silicon interval, 56.5 to
57.5, is also far narrower than the people's interval, 54.2 to 57.3, and it misses
the people's average entirely. A thousand generated answers make the estimate
precise, and it is a precise estimate of what the model says. That is the billing-error
lesson again: size shrinks the wobble and leaves the tilt in place.

None of this makes a language model useless to a survey researcher. It can be a useful
assistant for work that happens *before* you field a questionnaire. It can flag a
question that is confusing or double-barreled (asking two things at once), suggest
answer options you forgot, role-play a hurried respondent so you notice a skip that
makes no sense, or help you draft probes for a later round of **cognitive interviews**,
sessions in which real people answer a draft question and say aloud how they read it.
Example: a respondent explains that "household income" made her wonder whether to count
her roommate. Every one of
those uses improves an instrument that people will answer. What it cannot do is stand
in for the people. A silicon result reported as "voters feel..." is a **silent scope
change** from the model to a population whose answers nobody collected.

If a model's answers are what you want to describe, say so, and design for it: the
model is then your object of study, and the audit designs in
[Audit Studies](../part7-further-routes/audit-studies.qmd) show how to vary inputs and
count repeated outputs honestly. If you want to pretest the wording of a survey
experiment, [Survey Experiments](../part7-further-routes/survey-experiments.qmd)
shows where a pretest ends and a result begins.

## An AI failure case

You ask a chatbot: *"My survey of current subscribers shows a 2% billing-error rate on
a large panel. Can I report the service's billing-error rate as 2%?"* It answers with
full confidence: *"Yes. With a sample that large, your estimate is precise and
reliable."* This is wrong in two named ways at once. It commits a **silent scope
change**, quietly upgrading "current subscribers" to "the service's customers," and it
leans on the fallacy that a big sample cures a tilted one.

You catch it because you wrote your own answer first, and yours named the frame: the
customers still subscribed, not everyone the service bills, so the swap is visible on
sight. Then you check the mechanism against the data. The customers with the worst
billing errors canceled before the survey went out, so missingness relates directly to
the outcome you count. A larger panel of current subscribers only estimates the
current subscribers' error rate more precisely. It never reaches the people who left.

Commit your own answer first, then delegate. Each prompt below leaves the judgment
with you and hands the AI only the legwork. Work them as a loop rather than a
one-shot: the first list of dropout groups is always the obvious one, and the useful
answer usually arrives on the second or third pass, after you have told the tool which
group it missed and asked it to try again with that in mind.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three decisions stay yours alone. First, **which population your project is really
about**: the AI does not know your question's intent. Second, **which frame you can
honestly reach**, and therefore the coverage gap you must disclose. Third, **the
boundary line itself**: the exact sentence where your description stops and the
population claim you refuse to make. You may ask an AI to attack that line, never to
draw it for you.
:::

1. Decide which case you are in. Read your inquiry's words. If it asks *how much, how
   many, how often*, over a group you will observe rather than assign, this is your
   pathway. If it asks *why* or *what would happen if*, it is not, and you run the
   drill in step 5 instead.
2. **If this is your pathway**, write your four boxes, one line each: target
   population, accessible population, sampling frame, sample. Be concrete about the
   frame. Name the actual list, database, or feed your data will come from.
3. Draw your selection diagram: an arrow from each box to the next, with the filter
   that removes people written on the arrow. Circle the one filter you most fear bends
   *both* who you reach and what you measure. That is the one you will have to
   disclose.

   **List-to-verify.** Turn a vague worry into a checkable list of who drops out.

   ```
   I am drawing a selection diagram for an observational study. My target
   population is [X], my frame is [Y], my sample is [Z]. List each group that
   drops out between target and sample, in a table, with whether their absence
   pushes my estimate up or down.
   ```

   After running, verify by mapping each named group to one real step in your own
   diagram, and checking that the one group you feared most is on the list. Counters
   *illusion of completeness*: a long, tidy list that quietly omits the group that
   matters most.
4. Write the two sentences that define your claim. The first is the population claim
   your frame actually licenses, stated with its uncertainty. The second is the silent
   upgrade your design forbids, written out in full so you can recognize and refuse it
   when a coauthor or an AI hands it back to you.

   **Red-team.** Make the AI attack your boundary sentence instead of praising it.

   ```
   Here is a boundary sentence I wrote: "[your sentence]". Act as a hostile peer
   reviewer. Name every place it over-reaches, under-states the bias, or hides the
   direction of the drift. Do not rewrite it for me.
   ```

   After running, verify by checking each objection against your own numbers and pushing
   back if every objection is mild. Counters *sycophantic agreement*: an AI that calls
   your caveat "well-balanced" has reviewed your ego, not your evidence.
5. **If this is not your pathway**, run the classification drill instead. Write your
   question as if it were an observational descriptive question, name the four boxes it
   would need, and say precisely what that version could not tell you. The sentence
   you cannot write here is the reason your chosen pathway has to earn its extra
   assumptions.
6. Log the work in your AI Research Ledger, and verify the key claim with a named
   method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd); simulation fits
   here, because the claim is about how a sampling procedure behaves rather than about
   a fixed number. An AI reviewer may attack your boundary sentence with you; the
   decision to hold the line or move it stays yours.

   **Locate.** Find real methodological backing instead of trusting a paragraph.

   ```
   Act as a research-methods assistant. List real, retrievable references on
   survivorship and nonresponse bias in observational studies. For each, give
   title, authors, year, and venue, and mark any you are not confident exist.
   ```

   After running, verify by opening each source in a library database before you cite it.
   Counters *confident fabrication*: a fluent citation for a paper that does not exist
   looks identical to a real one until you try to retrieve it.
